title: The Capacity Gap: What a Missed Trade Day Really Costs a Building Business
linkedin:
A missed day on a building site rarely shows up as a missing day's pay.

It shows up three weeks later, in a job that quietly ran over budget for reasons nobody can quite explain.

That's the real cost of a capacity gap, and most trade and construction businesses have never actually measured it.

A quoted day rate assumes a full crew, on site, on time. When that assumption breaks, plant hire keeps running, site supervision keeps running, and the client's completion date doesn't move just because the roster did. A one-day gap becomes a rescheduled trade, a second site visit, sometimes a penalty clause. None of it arrives as a line item called "capacity shortfall." It just turns up later, quietly buried in a job that didn't make the margin it should have.

There's a quieter pattern underneath that. When the roster comes up short, the person who absorbs the gap is usually the owner. They pick up the tools, run the second site, work the weekend to keep the job on schedule.

It works, and it's exactly why the true cost of a capacity gap so rarely gets measured. The owner's unpaid labour masks it every time.

That backup role has a habit of becoming permanent long after the business can genuinely afford it, and it quietly caps growth, because the business can only take on as much work as the owner can personally cover when something goes wrong.

None of this means carrying idle headcount as insurance against a bad week. It means knowing the real number before the next gap happens, then deciding deliberately how much buffer is worth carrying.
